job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a room with my cousin Marco in a flat in Dunmore, close to the old industrial estate. Mornings I do applications and a bit of CAD practice, then I fix things around the flat or help my uncle in his garage. In the afternoon I play five-a-side with friends. It's a decent routine, but it's not a job, and everyone at family dinners asks me about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. Tell me about your degree and what you did for your internship.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanical engineering at Calder University. My final project was a gearbox for a student racing team, which broke twice and then worked. I also spent eight weeks on the maintenance team at a packaging factory, helping plan machine servicing, which taught me more than any lecture. I'm looking for a design or maintenance engineering job at a manufacturer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, that matches what I saw at the factory: software that helps a bit, but a machine still jams and someone has to fix it. To friends I'd say don't believe every headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my main problem is the same as before, no first offer. There are plenty of manufacturers near Dunmore, but they want someone with two years of experience, and my eight weeks isn't that. I've got savings for about six or seven months, which is not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, ten a week, and I'd phone the maintenance manager from my internship, Mrs Kaplan, to ask if she has a vacancy. I'd learn a free tool called a PLC simulator, since many factories use that kind of controller. I'd use AI tools for tidying my CV, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It isn't dramatic, it's the dull worry of waiting on other people to decide about you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine still jams. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the packaging line, the software could predict a failure maybe half the time. The other half, a bearing seized and Mrs Kaplan's team had to stand there with spanners. I saw that and I trust it more than any presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job outside engineering if it came up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider it for a few months, like a warehouse planner role, as long as it keeps me near machines. I wouldn't wait forever for the perfect post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real change but not the end of the world. At family dinners I'd say that the desk part of engineering will change a lot, and the workshop part not much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think design and calculation work, the entry-level stuff, is exactly what these tools handle first. So graduate design roles shrink, but maintenance and hands-on roles hold. That points me toward the workshop side more than I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my search toward maintenance, commissioning and service engineering roles. I'd add a short course on industrial controls and I'd use AI tools more often, especially for calculations and report writing. I'd also tell my uncle that I might take a few months of work in his garage if nothing comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My own job is likely to be fewer and later, and my savings are what stand between me and a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI tools more often. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I only use them to check my writing. I'd start using one for calculations and reading datasheets, and I'd check every answer by hand. Mrs Kaplan's rule was that you never trust a number you didn't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first if the search failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership and the weekend trips. I'd keep the phone because I apply from it. Marco and I would also move to a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, by 2028, is far too quick for anyone to react sensibly. I'd say we need honest numbers from governments and employers, and an income floor in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be alarmed. Design work and the desk side of engineering is thinking work, so it goes first. My hands-on route holds until about 2031, but companies would stop hiring graduates well before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job near machines, a technician post, an apprenticeship, whatever pays, and I'd get a trade qualification like an electrician's ticket. I'd keep my savings in cash and cut everything extra. I'd also ask my uncle about taking over part of the garage's servicing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, yes. I'd keep a calm face for the family, but I'd be counting every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd get an electrician's qualification. Why that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to wire the robots and the sites, and it's work that has to be done in a particular building. It's the kind of job I'd put in the safe pile for the extra three years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco, who works in an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To start a plan B this week, like a night course in anything physical. He wouldn't like hearing it, but I'd tell him straight.

I'd say so to anyone who asks.
think: Design is thinking work, so it goes **first**, and graduate hiring would stop before 2031.
My hands-on route holds a little **longer**.

Get a **trade qualification**, such as an electrician's.
Keep savings in cash and ask my uncle about garage **servicing** work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd call fast but manageable if people start early. I'd say that employers need to say what roles will look like in 2031, not wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's roughly a fair window. If I get a first job within a year, I'd have four years of experience, and a good record in maintenance should be valuable when robots arrive around 2034. I worry about the first rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job as soon as I can, in maintenance or commissioning, and add an evening course in robotics maintenance. I'd put aside half my pay in a savings account and an index fund. I'd also keep contact with my internship team so I'm known when positions open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a route, and I'd still be quite nervous the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why robotics maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots reach hands-on work in 2034, someone has to fix the robots. It's what I've seen at the factory, only with a different machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the first year easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A manager who'll explain what they expect, and one colleague who'll show me where the spare parts are. That's the kind of thing that matters on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to do things properly. I'd say it's an opportunity, and that the main job is making sure people actually use the time rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's quite calm. I'd have a career, chartered status perhaps, and a decent savings pot by 2036. I'd probably be in maintenance or operations at a manufacturer, which is hands-on enough to last until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, work my way up and add certificates every couple of years. I'd learn AI tools as they become useful for planning maintenance. I'd also help my uncle's garage move to electric vehicle servicing, since that's coming whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. Ten years is something to plan for, not to dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people wait instead of using the time. Do you do that yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I tell myself I'll plan properly once I have a job, which is a nice excuse. This interview is making me think I should make a list tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get hired, find a mentor, put a fixed amount into savings, and one new certificate. Nothing dramatic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives no time. In the others I can picture a path, but in that one even my sensible plans are guesses. What would help is employers being honest about hiring, and some kind of income cushion during the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that most of us in the middle aren't shouting about this. We're quietly working out what to do, and we'd like someone to ask us.

headlineQuote: Most of us in the middle aren't shouting about this. We're quietly working out what to do
portrait: Diego is a **23-year-old** mechanical engineering graduate sharing a room with his cousin, still waiting on a first offer.
He is a **pragmatic centrist** who judges each scenario by evidence, and his factory internship taught him where machines really fit.
He tries AI tools **now and then** and adopts them once they've proved useful, so he moves steadily rather than first.
His mood is **uneasy** or anxious in most scenarios and alarmed only when the 2028 clock leaves no room to plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because even his sensible plans would be guesses.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **hiring information** from employers and an **income cushion** during the change.
